text: Paroxetine is a strong inhibitor of CYP2D6.
Paroxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
Paroxetine is associated with discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly.
Paroxetine has anticholinergic activity relative to other SSRIs.
Metoprolol is metabolised principally by CYP2D6.
Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective adrenergic blocker.
Metoprolol is used in heart failure and after myocardial infarction.
Metoprolol is available as tartrate and succinate salts.

Yes. Paroxetine is a strong inhibitor of CYP2D6, and metoprolol is metabolised principally by CYP2D6, with extensive first-pass metabolism dependent on this enzyme. Co-administration means paroxetine will inhibit metoprolol's CYP2D6-mediated metabolism, reducing both first-pass clearance and systemic clearance. This increases metoprolol plasma concentrations, which can produce exaggerated beta-blockade — bradycardia, hypotension, dizziness — and this interaction is clinically recognised as significant. Dose reduction of metoprolol or switching to a non-CYP2D6-dependent beta-blocker is typically advised.

MECHANISM: Paroxetine strongly inhibits CYP2D6, decreasing metabolism of metoprolol (a CYP2D6 substrate) and raising its exposure
FINAL ANSWER: YES
